statement: A running model, not a calibrated one. Its numbers are chosen for this rose from what the breeder, the RHS and growers say of it (its height, the size of its flowers, its season, how a climbing rose is trained and pruned) and from one measured garden rose of another cultivar; none has been measured on a plant of 'The Generous Gardener'. It flowers on side shoots from canes that a gardener has tied in, and shows repeat flowering as a steady succession, not as flushes. Use its output to compare scenarios and to show what a design implies, not to predict dates, sizes or loads.

names.basis: A spray carries on the line of the side shoot it ends, and its flowers nod on their own stalks: the breeder describes flowers that "nod gracefully on the stem" (https://www.davidaustinroses.co.uk/products/the-generous-gardener-climbing-rose). The nodding is drawn by the flower model. That the hips are held where the flowers were is assumed: a hip is the swollen base of the flower it follows.

phenology.budburstDoy.basis: Early March. No dated record of this cultivar breaking bud was found. The RHS has climbing roses pruned between December and February, before growth starts, and fed in March or April "before flowering" (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide, https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/growing-guide); David Austin describes roses responding "with remarkable vigour" as the days lengthen through spring (https://eu.davidaustinroses.com/blogs/news/what-the-longest-day-reveals-about-roses). The day is a choice inside that.

phenology.growthEndDoy.basis: Mid October. A repeat-flowering rose goes on making flowering growth into autumn: "a late flourish in October, or even November" (https://www.crocus.co.uk/features/_/articleid.1321/). No measured date; the engine also spreads the year's extension evenly between budburst and this day, which a rose that grows in flushes does not do.

phenology.leafFlushDoy.basis: Leaves open from mid March to the end of April as the shoots of the year lengthen. A choice that follows from the budburst date; not observed. Nearly every leaf of this plant stands on growth of the year, and opens as that growth is made, so this window matters only to the nursery cane.

phenology.autumnColourDoy.basis: November. Garden roses of this kind keep their leaves late and yellow a little before they drop; no source read describes autumn colour in this cultivar, and none is claimed for it. The dates are a choice.

phenology.leafFallDoy.basis: Mid November to Christmas. The RHS lists the plant as deciduous (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/196207/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn-cl/details) and has climbing roses pruned from December and renovated "when the rose is leafless" between late autumn and late winter (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide). In mild winters some leaves hang on longer than this; the engine treats the plant as fully deciduous.

phenology.floralInitiationDoy.basis: A rose forms its flower buds at the tips of the shoots of the year as they grow, with no resting stage; they show about a month before they open. The second day is the one on which the engine gives each flowering side shoot its bud (20 May), a little before the first flowers of June. No dated source.

phenology.flowerOpenDoy.basis: 6 June to 20 October: the envelope inside which any flower of the plant opens. The breeder: "Repeat flowering", in flushes "from late spring to early winter" (https://www.davidaustinroses.co.uk/products/the-generous-gardener-climbing-rose). Repeat-flowering roses give "a main flush in June" with "five to six weeks between flushes" and "a late flourish in October, or even November" (https://www.crocus.co.uk/features/_/articleid.1321/); David Austin: "By late June, many varieties are producing an abundance of blooms" (https://eu.davidaustinroses.com/blogs/news/what-the-longest-day-reveals-about-roses); the RHS: "repeat-flowering from midsummer to autumn" (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/196207/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn-cl/details). The first flowers open in the June flush (flowering.firstFlushDays) and the later ones follow the flowers before them (flowering.repeat*), so the window bounds the season and does not spread the flowers over it.

phenology.petalFallDoy.basis: Not used: each spray lasts phenology.flowerLastsDays from the day it opens. Present because every model carries every parameter; the window is the opening window moved on by the life of a spray.

phenology.flowerLastsDays.basis: How long one spray is in flower: its two to four flowers open in succession ("Flowers open in succession", https://eu.davidaustinroses.com/blogs/news/what-the-longest-day-reveals-about-roses) and each lasts some days. Growers say single blooms of this cultivar "fall apart quickly" (https://www.helpmefind.com/gardening/l.php?l=2.37005&tab=32). No count of days was found; a choice.

extension.leaderMPerSeason.basis: Length a main cane adds in a full season. The breeder gives the plant 15 ft (4.5 m), the height of "a 3-year-old established rose, pruned once a year" (https://www.davidaustinroses.co.uk/products/the-generous-gardener-climbing-rose), and the RHS "up to 4.5m" (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/196207/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn-cl/details), in a size band reached in 5 to 10 years; one grower records a first-year plant "growing 12 feet tall by the end of the summer" and another that it took "many seasons" to make canes long enough to climb (https://www.helpmefind.com/gardening/l.php?l=2.37005&tab=32). A height is not a growth rate: 2.2 m a season is a choice that brings a cane to its length in about three seasons.

extension.lateralMPerSeasonByOrder.basis: Branch canes are taken to grow more slowly than the main canes they spring from. Not measured.

extension.whipMPerSeason.basis: Not used: this model throws no free long shoots (organs.whipShareOfNodes is 0). Present because every model carries every parameter.

extension.establishmentFactorByYear.basis: A newly planted rose is taken to make half its later growth in its first season and four fifths in its second, while it roots. No measured figure for a rose; a choice.

architecture.trunkStemStartYears.basis: Two canes on the plant as it comes from the nursery, then a new cane from the base in each of the next three seasons and one more in the sixth: six in all. The RHS, renovating a climbing rose, keeps "no more than six young, vigorous stems" (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide). The engine never takes an old cane out, as a gardener does, so six is where it stops.

architecture.nurseryCaneM.basis: A bare-root or potted climbing rose arrives cut back to short canes. Not measured.

architecture.maxBranchOrder.basis: Main canes carry branch canes, which carry one further order. The short flowering side shoots are counted apart (sideShoots).

architecture.leaderLengthM.basis: The length at which a main cane stops. The breeder gives 15 ft (4.5 m) as a climber (https://www.davidaustinroses.co.uk/products/the-generous-gardener-climbing-rose), the RHS "up to 4.5m" (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/196207/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn-cl/details), HelpMeFind 150 to 450 cm (https://www.helpmefind.com/rose/l.php?l=2.37005). Those are heights; a cane tied along a lattice is longer than the height it reaches, so this is a choice of that order and not a reading.

architecture.lateralLengthMByOrder.basis: Branch canes are taken to be about a third the length of a main cane, and theirs half that again. Not measured.

architecture.lateralLengthSpread.basis: Branch canes vary in length by about a third either way. Not measured.

architecture.lateralChanceByParentOrder.basis: The chance that a cane tied past a crossing of the lattice later throws a branch cane there. A climbing rose branches from its tied-in canes, the more so where they are bent towards the level; how often has not been counted. A choice that fills the specimen frame with a framework of the order a trained plant has, not a thicket.

architecture.budExtraDormancyChance.basis: Half the buds that will make a branch cane wait a year or more before they do, so that the framework fills over several years. No source for a rose; a choice.

architecture.maxStemsPerRoute.basis: Canes a gardener ties along one lath or cable. The RHS spaces training wires 30 cm apart (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide); two canes to a member is a choice for a lattice whose members are farther apart than that.

architecture.maxStemsPerPrimaryMember.basis: As architecture.maxStemsPerRoute: a gardener does not bundle canes on a glulam member either.

routing.occupancyCost.basis: A rose goes where it is tied. The gardener fans the canes out over the support, so a member that already carries a cane is the less likely to be given another. A choice.

routing.downhillCostPerM.basis: A cane is rarely tied downwards. A choice.

routing.uphillBonusPerM.basis: The gardener leads canes upwards, but less eagerly than a twiner climbs: the RHS trains the main shoots of a climbing rose "as horizontal as possible" to make them flower low down (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide). A choice.

routing.straightOnBonus.basis: A cane is stiff and is tied on along the line it is growing in where it can be. A choice.

routing.riserBonus.basis: The first cane is led up to the top of the support. A choice.

routing.tierBonus.basis: The other canes are tied along the level members, as the RHS advises (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide). A choice.

routing.roleDropChance.basis: How often the gardener changes the line of a cane at a crossing. A choice.

routing.noise.basis: The unevenness of one gardener's tying-in from cane to cane. A choice.

routing.giveUpCost.basis: A cane with nowhere to go but steeply down is stopped. A choice.

attachment.maxGraspDiameterMm.basis: Not used: a rose cannot hold on by itself and is tied wherever it goes.

attachment.minPitchM.basis: Not applicable to a rose: it does not twine. Present because every model carries every parameter.

attachment.pitchPerCircumference.basis: Not applicable to a rose: it does not twine. Present because every model carries every parameter.

organs.leafSpacingM.basis: Stem between one leaf and the next. On a measured garden rose of another cultivar ('Radrazz') the internodes of a flowering shoot were 1 to 63.5 mm, about 12 to 34 mm in mid shoot (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2013.00418/full); the long canes of a climber are longer-jointed than that. One spacing serves both the canes and the flowering side shoots of this model; the flowering shoot's is taken, because those shoots carry nearly all the leaves, so a cane in its first year is leafier than it should be. The engine lays stem in 40 mm steps and sets a leaf no closer than that. Not measured on this cultivar.

organs.leafLengthM.basis: The whole leaf, stalk to the tip of the end leaflet. HelpMeFind and NC State call the foliage "large" (https://www.helpmefind.com/rose/l.php?l=2.37005, https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn/); NC State puts the leaflets in its 1 to 3 inch class. A leaf of five or seven leaflets 4 to 6 cm long is 11 to 17 cm long. Not measured on this cultivar.

organs.leavesPerNode.basis: NC State Extension plant record: leaf arrangement "Alternate". One leaf to a node.

organs.spurChance.basis: A rose has no flowering spurs: it flowers at the ends of leafy side shoots (sideShoots).

organs.spurLengthM.basis: Not applicable to a rose: see organs.spurChance. Present because every model carries every parameter.

organs.spurLeafCount.basis: Not applicable to a rose: see organs.spurChance.

organs.racemeLengthM.basis: The width of a spray across its flowers: up to three open flowers and a bud or two, each flower of the breeder's "medium" bloom size, 2 to 3.5 inches (5 to 9 cm) (https://www.davidaustinroses.co.uk/products/the-generous-gardener-climbing-rose); HelpMeFind gives an average bloom diameter of 2.5 inches and "in small clusters" (https://www.helpmefind.com/rose/l.php?l=2.37005). About two and a half flowers wide. The width of a spray is not given by any source: it is worked out from the bloom size.

organs.whipShareOfNodes.basis: No free long shoots. The long shoots a climbing rose makes each year are the canes a gardener ties in, which this model grows as tied canes; those left over are tied in or shortened in autumn (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide). The engine has no routine that does that for a rose, and a shoot it left would stand bare for ever, so none is thrown.

organs.whipLengthM.basis: Not used: see organs.whipShareOfNodes. Present because every model carries every parameter.

organs.leafLifespanYears.basis: RHS plant record: foliage "Deciduous". A leaf lasts the season it grew in.

organs.clearStemHeightM.basis: The base of a climbing rose is bare: the RHS sets the lowest training wire 45 cm above the ground (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide), and a grower of this cultivar reports "hardly any leaves until you get to the top of the plant" (https://www.helpmefind.com/gardening/l.php?l=2.37005&tab=32). A choice of that order.

flowering.competenceYears.basis: Flowers from its second summer: the side shoots that flower break from canes made the year before. A rose planted in spring may give a few flowers in its first summer; the model gives none.

flowering.maturityRamp.basis: A young plant is taken to flower on fewer of its side shoots. Not measured.

flowering.spurFloralChance.basis: Not applicable to a rose: it has no spurs.

flowering.unprunedFactor.basis: Not applicable to a rose: this factor belongs to spur pruning.

flowering.currentSeasonFlowersPerM.basis: No flowers along the canes themselves. A rose flowers at the end of a leafy shoot, never from a leaf node of a long cane, so every flower of this model is the spray at the end of a side shoot (sideShoots.terminalFlowerShare). In life a strong new cane may also end in a spray late in its first summer; that is left out.

pruning.summerLeavesKept.basis: Not applicable to a rose: this is the summer cut of a spur-pruned plant. Present because every model carries every parameter.

pruning.winterBudsKept.basis: Not applicable to a rose: this is the winter cut of a spur-pruned plant. Present because every model carries every parameter.

regrowth.shootsPerCut.basis: A rose cane cut hard breaks from the buds below the cut, commonly two or three of them. Not counted on this cultivar.

thickening.tipRadiusSquaredMm2.basis: A shoot 3.2 mm thick where it is new: of the order of the stalk under a spray and the tip of a side shoot. A cane tip is stouter than this. Not measured.

thickening.radiusSquaredPerMetreMm2.basis: Gives a main cane that carries ten metres of branch canes a base about 20 mm thick, which is of the order of the old canes of a climbing rose. Not measured.

thickening.branchShare.basis: A branch cane adds nearly all of its own section to the cane that bears it. Not measured.

fruit.setShare.basis: The share of sprays left on the plant that leave hips. The cultivar sets them where the spent flowers are left: "lovely orange hips in the autumn" (https://www.provendernurseries.co.uk/factsheets/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn); a vase of its hips, "rather fat and rosy orange", was picked in late December (https://teddingtongardener.com/2013/12/22). How freely it sets them has not been counted. A spray the gardener deadheads leaves none (the routine deadheads until late August).

fruit.lengthM.basis: The length of the cluster of hips a spray leaves, from the end of the side shoot to the far end of the hips: a main stalk of about 3 cm, a stalk of about 5 cm to each hip and a hip of 18 to 26 mm. No source gives the size of the hips: the only measure found is NC State's 1 to 3 inch class (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn/) and "rather fat" (https://teddingtongardener.com/2013/12/22). Worked out from those, not measured.

fruit.swellDays.basis: A hip is taken to reach its size five to seven weeks after the petals fall. Not measured.

fruit.ripenDoy.basis: Hips colour between early September and the end of November: "orange hips in the autumn" (https://www.provendernurseries.co.uk/factsheets/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn). Hips set by the last flowers of the year are full grown too late to colour, and stay green until they go with their shoot.

fruit.fallDoy.basis: Hips hang on the bare plant through the winter (picked in late December: https://teddingtongardener.com/2013/12/22; a winter food for thrushes and blackbirds: https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/growing-guide) and are taken to go between late January and early March, before growth starts. Not observed.

appendages.tendrilNodePattern.basis: Not applicable to a rose: it has no tendrils.

appendages.tendrilLengthM.basis: Not applicable to a rose: see appendages.tendrilNodePattern.

appendages.leafStalkCoilShare.basis: Not applicable to a rose: its leaf stalks do not coil.

appendages.leafStalkLengthM.basis: Not applicable to a rose: see appendages.leafStalkCoilShare.

appendages.aerialRootPatchSpacingM.basis: Not applicable to a rose: it makes no clinging rootlets.

appendages.aerialRootLengthM.basis: Not applicable to a rose: see appendages.aerialRootPatchSpacingM.

appendages.prickleSpacingM.basis: Stem between one prickle and the next. Sources disagree about how armed this cultivar is: NC State calls it "nearly prickle-free" (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rosa-the-generous-gardener-ausdrawn/), while growers call it "thorny, but not more than a normal thorny rose" and the taxon file records thorns as a hazard near the public. The model takes the cautious reading, a moderately armed cane. Not counted on a plant.

appendages.prickleLengthM.basis: Not measured on this cultivar. The prickles of another climbing rose, Rosa arvensis 'Splendens', were 4.8 mm high (quartiles 4.4 to 5.4) on slender shoots and 7.5 mm (6.2 to 8.4) on stout ones (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4667892/); the range spans the two.

sideShoots.bearingWoodAgeYears.basis: The flowering side shoots of a climbing rose break from canes made in an earlier year: the RHS keeps the framework and shortens the "flowered side shoots" each winter (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide).

sideShoots.perMetrePerYear.basis: About half the buds along an older cane break into a side shoot each spring. On a cane trained towards the level nearly every bud breaks, on an upright one only the uppermost; the engine does not tell the two apart. Not counted on a plant.

sideShoots.lengthM.basis: A flowering shoot of a measured garden rose of another cultivar had 10 to 16 leaves on internodes of about 12 to 34 mm (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2013.00418/full), which is a shoot of this order. Not measured on this cultivar.

sideShoots.lifespanYears.basis: A side shoot flowers in the summer it grows. Left alone, the engine sheds it at the next budburst and starts another from the cane. Where the gardener has shortened it in winter (the RHS cuts flowered side shoots back by two thirds, https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/roses/climbing/pruning-guide, and new ones break from what is left) the stub stays, and the next side shoot breaks from its top.

sideShoots.terminalFlowerShare.basis: Three side shoots in four end in a spray; the rest are blind. Not counted on a plant.

flowering.firstFlushDays.basis: The first flowers at the ends of the side shoots open from 6 to 30 June: "a main flush in June" (https://www.crocus.co.uk/features/_/articleid.1321/); the breeder's main flush is in June (SPECIES_PROFILE.md, flowering season). How many days the flush is spread over was not found for this cultivar; three and a half weeks is a choice.

flowering.repeatMaxPerSeason.basis: A June flush, then flushes "five to six weeks" apart to "a late flourish in October, or even November" (https://www.crocus.co.uk/features/_/articleid.1321/): from late June to October that is three more at most. Not counted on this cultivar.

flowering.repeatIntervalDays.basis: From a spray going over, left on the plant, to the next flower at the same place: two weeks longer than after deadheading. The breeder deadheads repeat-flowering climbers so that "they never stall" (https://davidaustinroses.co.uk/blogs/rose-care/how-to-deadhead-a-rose), and a spray left to set hips is taken to hold the next back. How much is a choice; no interval was found measured.

flowering.repeatIntervalDeadheadedDays.basis: "Five to six weeks between flushes" (https://www.crocus.co.uk/features/_/articleid.1321/), read as from the opening of one flush to the opening of the next. A spray of this rose is in flower for 16 to 26 days (phenology.flowerLastsDays), so from the deadheading of a spray that has gone over to the next flower at the same place is about two to four weeks. Read instead as from the end of one flush to the next it would be three weeks longer; the source does not say which it means. Not measured on this cultivar.

flowering.repeatShare.basis: Each flush lesser than the last: half the places that flowered flower again, so the flushes go one, a half, a quarter, an eighth. Growers of this cultivar find later bloom "sporadic, into September and October, but nothing like the main flush" (https://www.helpmefind.com/gardening/l.php?l=2.37005&tab=32). The share is a choice, not a count.

sideShoots.baseDiameterMm.basis: A flowering side shoot of 0.6 m, the longest the model makes, 6 mm thick at its foot while it grows, tapering to the 3.2 mm of a new tip (thickening.tipRadiusSquaredMm2): about the thickness of a pencil, which is the size of flowering wood a rose gardener keeps. No measurement of a side shoot of this or any climbing rose was found; a choice.

mechanics.inflorescenceFreshMassKg.basis: A spray of one to three open flowers and a bud or two (SPECIES_PROFILE.md). Worked out, not weighed: whole flowers of small-flowered diploid roses with 14 to 22 petals weighed 0.2 to 0.3 g fresh (Rawandoozi and others 2023, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1226713); a flower of this rose has 40 to 50 petals and is 5 to 9 cm across, about twice the petals and four times the petal area, which puts a flower at about 4 to 6 g with its receptacle and stalk, and a spray of two open flowers and one and a half buds at about 12 g. Rain on the petals, which can double it, is not a load in the model.

mechanics.fruitFreshMassKg.basis: A cluster of one to three hips (SPECIES_PROFILE.md), two on average. Worked out, not weighed: hips of Rosa canina weighed 1.9 to 3.0 g fresh, plant by plant (Sindrak and others 2012, https://hrcak.srce.hr/clanak/123964), at about 13 to 17 mm across; a hip of this rose is 18 to 26 mm and "rather fat", about two and a half times the volume, so about 5 to 6 g, and a cluster of two about 12 g with its stalks. No hip of this cultivar was weighed.
